30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 25: Going Live — Deploying to GitHub Pages
"If nobody else can see it, you're just impressing yourself."
Yep. No matter how useful the project you've been building is, it still only lives at
, an address that only your own computer knows about.
So today I'm going to show you how to use GitHub Pages to put your project out there, so other people can see it and actually use it.
I'm guessing a lot of people's first reaction is: "Why GitHub Pages?"
It's pretty simple. Our project is a front-end project — no back end, no database, no login — so anywhere that can host static files will work.
And there are three reasons I picked GitHub Pages:
All you need is a GitHub account, so there's no extra service to sign up for.
GitHub Pages gives you roughly 100GB of bandwidth a month, which is plenty for a small project.
GitHub Actions can automate deployment. After you push, it builds, uploads, and deploys on its own, so you skip the hassle of uploading by hand.
Overall, you don't need to spend extra time learning Cloudflare Pages or Vercel. GitHub alone covers everything we need.
You're also going to see the word "build" a lot in a minute. In short, it means packaging our app into a bundle of purely static files (HTML, CSS, JS). The packaged files go into a folder called
, and "deploying" really just means putting that folder on GitHub Pages.

GitHub is a third-party code hosting platform. Its Pages feature is free, but it isn't built specifically for hosting websites. If your project is commercial or gets a lot of traffic, I'd recommend finding a service made for that. This post is only meant for practice or personal projects.

So is that it? Are we done?
Nope. So far we've only "hosted" the code on GitHub. It isn't actually deployed to GitHub Pages yet.
So once the project's pushed, we'll ask the AI to set up a GitHub Actions workflow that handles deployment for us automatically.

In normal development, we split work into branches — a development branch, a testing branch, a production branch, and so on. In most real projects, only the Main branch (or Master branch) gets deployed to production, and the other branches are for testing environments.
What about us? Do we need that? Not yet, unless you're really curious about it. So we'll just stick with the default branch (Main): push to Main, and it deploys automatically.
All you need to do is tell the AI this:

There's one more thing to adjust before you push, though. Go to your GitHub repo → Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source, and pick GitHub Actions. New repositories don't have Pages turned on by default, so if you skip this, Actions will throw an error in a minute.
If everything looks fine so far, ask the AI to commit the current progress and push it to GitHub, and you'll see Actions start running.
If Actions throws an error along the way, it's almost always because you forgot to change the Pages Source in your repo. Go back, fix that setting, and push again.
If everything went smoothly, your project is now officially live for the world to see!
